olm8ij-g51791-d1e103.summary: Rubric for Distinction 23 of Book III. Its printed title, 'De modo unionis ex parte assumentis' (on the mode of union on the part of the one assuming), is a running label and does not match the item's actual topic. It makes no argument.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e116.summary: Rubric labelling the item as Question 1.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e128.summary: Rubric for the single article: whether a divine person could assume a man without quantity.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e137.summary: Opening argument for the negative. Quantity cannot be assumed without a subject, so neither can material substance be assumed without quantity. What is more often found separated from something is more easily assumed without it. Quantity is found without substance (in the Eucharist), but material substance is never found without quantity. Proof of the premise: an accident can inhere only in what it perfects and informs. Quantity cannot perfect a divine person, since that person would then be in potency to an accident. So quantity can neither inhere in nor depend on a divine supposit, and cannot be assumed by it.
claims: Quantity cannot be assumed by a divine person.
An accident inheres only in what it perfects and informs.
A divine person cannot be in potency to an accident.
Material substance, never found without quantity, is harder to assume without it than quantity without substance.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e194.summary: Counters an anticipated reply. The reply says quantity could depend on and inhere in a supposit without perfecting or informing it, since depending is prior to perfecting. Against this: depending and perfecting are essentially linked. Informing cannot occur without depending, so depending cannot occur without informing. It is even more impossible for an accident to inhere without perfecting, and nothing can perfect a subject without depending on it. Otherwise the Holy Spirit could perfect the will without depending on it, which contradicts the common view. So quantity cannot inhere in or be assumed by a divine supposit.
claims: Dependence on a subject and perfecting it are essentially connected.
An accident cannot inhere in a subject without perfecting it.
Quantity cannot be assumed by a divine supposit.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e245.summary: Argument for the affirmative. Human nature depends more truly on its supposit, and forms a more genuine unity with it, than substance does with quantity. Nature and supposit make something one per se, with nature in essential potency to the supposit. Substance and quantity make something one only per accidens. Since a nature can be assumed without its own supposit, a man can all the more be assumed without quantity.
claims: Nature and supposit make a per se unity; substance and quantity make a per accidens unity.
Human nature can be assumed without its proper supposit.
A man can therefore all the more be assumed without quantity.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e280.summary: Presents an opposing opinion: it is impossible, even for God, to assume a man without quantity. First reason: what cannot actually exist without something cannot be assumed without it. A man cannot exist without quantity. A determinate form requires determinate matter (De anima II: the acts of agents are in a rightly disposed patient). The intellective soul's proper matter is an organic physical body, which cannot actually exist without quantity.
claims: What cannot actually exist without X cannot be assumed without X.
A determinate form requires determinate matter.
The intellective soul requires an organic physical body, which is necessarily quantified.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e328.summary: Second reason for the opposing opinion. It belongs per se to man to be an animal, to an animal to be sensible, and to a sensible being to be organic, since sensing needs an organ. Organs require quantity. So a man cannot actually exist, or be assumed, without quantity.
claims: Sensation requires an organ, and organs require quantity.
Man cannot exist or be assumed without quantity.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e350.summary: Third reason for the opposing opinion. Some accidents, such as mathematical ones like quantity, determine their subject, yet can be separated from it (as quantity in the Eucharist). Likewise some forms determine certain accidents in their matter and cannot be separated from them. The intellective soul determines quantity in its matter, so it cannot exist in matter without quantity. It does not determine accidents such as whiteness or blackness, which is why man can be without those.
claims: Some forms determine certain accidents in matter and cannot be separated from them.
The intellective soul determines quantity in its matter.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e392.summary: Aureol summarizes the opposing opinion and disagrees with it. Because he sees no contradiction in it, he holds that God could assume a man without quantity. He introduces his clarification, which also refutes the opinion.
claims: God could assume a man without quantity, since doing so involves no contradiction.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e410.summary: Key distinction: man can be considered as a natural being, as the natural philosopher treats and defines him, or as a metaphysical being, as the metaphysician does. As a natural being, man cannot be assumed without quantity, since quantity falls in his definition in natural philosophy. Aureol bases this on how the sciences differ in abstraction (Physics II). The dialectician abstracts from quantity and quality. The metaphysician abstracts from sensible quality (but, as printed, not from quantity, apparently an error). The natural philosopher abstracts from neither sensible quantity nor quality.
claims: Man can be considered as a natural being or as a metaphysical being.
Quantity falls in the definition of man as a natural being.
As a natural being, man cannot exist or be assumed without quantity.
The sciences differ by their degree of abstraction from quantity and quality.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e481.summary: Supporting argument. Quality and quantity stand to the natural philosopher's consideration as act and potency stand to the metaphysician's. Nothing falls under natural philosophy without quality and quantity. So man, as natural philosophy treats him, cannot be or be assumed without quantity.
claims: Quality and quantity are proportional, for natural philosophy, to act and potency for metaphysics.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e501.summary: Further argument. If the natural philosopher considered composite substance precisely, without any accident, he would not differ from the metaphysician. Matter would not enter into the composition. If he considered substance only with quantity, he would not differ from the mathematician. So natural philosophy considers substance with quantity and quality, and man so considered cannot be found or assumed without quantity.
claims: Natural philosophy considers composite substance with its accidents.
This distinguishes natural philosophy from both metaphysics and mathematics.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e534.summary: Authorities for the natural-philosophical claim. Aristotle (De anima II) defines the soul as the act of an organic physical body, and an organic body needs quantity. So man as a natural being includes in his notion an accident as well as matter and form. Averroes confirms this (Metaphysics VII, comm. 37): man cannot be understood without flesh and bones, which are quantified. In comm. 39 he adds that natural things cannot be understood without motions and active and passive qualities.
claims: The soul is the act of an organic physical body (Aristotle).
Man as a natural being includes accidents in his notion.
Natural things cannot be understood without flesh, bones, motions and qualities (Averroes).

olm8ij-g51791-d1e581.summary: Aureol states his thesis. Considered by the natural philosopher, man cannot exist or be assumed without quantity. Considered as a metaphysical being, he can be assumed without quantity. First proof: the soul is related to the body both as form and as mover. The relation as form is prior and more essential. So the soul can give the body first being, as form, without moving it or giving it second acts such as sensing. Man can therefore be assumed without any quantity and without second acts.
claims: Man as a metaphysical being can be assumed without quantity.
The soul relates to the body both as form and as mover, and the relation as form is prior.
The soul can give first being without giving second acts such as sensation.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e633.summary: Qualification: a man assumed in this way would be neither wholly natural nor wholly metaphysical. He lacks quantity, but his matter is naturally apt for quantity and natural quality. Unlike an angel, he keeps a natural inclination to such accidents, just as the separated soul is neither wholly natural nor wholly metaphysical. Aureol then turns his opponents' own view against them: they hold that matter can exist without any form because matter has an essence and absolute nature distinct from the being of form.
claims: A man assumed without quantity would be neither wholly natural nor wholly metaphysical.
Such a man would retain a natural inclination to quantity and quality.
The separated soul is likewise intermediate between natural and metaphysical being.
The opponents grant that matter can exist without any form.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e679.summary: Develops the ad hominem argument. If matter can exist without form, then man, a complete soul-body composite distinct from quantity, can more readily exist without quantity. The more truly things are one, the harder they are to separate. Matter and form make a per se unity, man and quantity only a per accidens unity. Further, Aristotle (Metaphysics VII) says substance is prior to accident in definition, nature and time. Averroes infers from this that substance can be separated from accident, not accident from substance. Since accident can exist without substance, substance can all the more exist, and be assumed, without accident.
claims: The truer a unity, the less separable its parts.
Matter and form are a per se unity; man and quantity a per accidens unity.
Substance is prior to accident in definition, nature and time.
If accident can exist without substance, substance can all the more exist without accident.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e754.summary: Two more ad hominem arguments from the opponents' treatment of matter without form. First, form is the form of matter but not its formal cause, since matter is not matter by form. Likewise quantity gives accidental being to substance but is not its formal cause, so substance can be assumed without it. Second, matter has a divine idea distinct from that of form and so can exist without form. Complete substance and quantity are of different genera and have even more distinct ideas, so substance can be separated from quantity.
claims: Quantity is not the formal cause of substance.
Things with distinct divine ideas can exist separately.
Substance and quantity have distinct divine ideas because they are of different genera.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e796.summary: Final ad hominem argument and conclusion. Matter is capable of form but is not identical with that capacity. Likewise substance is capable of quantity but is not its capacity, so it can be separated from quantity. Aureol concludes that man, taken as matter and substantial form under metaphysical consideration, can be assumed without quantity. Such a man would be neither wholly natural nor wholly metaphysical, keeping a natural inclination to quantity and quality. He then turns to the opening arguments.
claims: Substance is capable of quantity but is not that capacity.
Man under metaphysical consideration can be assumed without quantity.
Such a man would retain a natural inclination to quantity and quality.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e838.summary: Reply to the first opening argument. Aureol denies the inference from quantity to substance. What is not personable or hypostasizable, such as an accident, cannot be assumed into unity of person. A personable nature like man can be. He also denies the premise, holding that an accident can be assumed. Quantity depends on another's supposit more than human nature does: even when it exists on its own (in the Eucharist) it keeps a natural inclination to a subject. So quantity could be sustained by, and assumed into, another's supposit. He then reformulates: an irrational nature cannot be assumed into unity of person but can be assumed into unity of hypostasis.
claims: An accident is neither personable nor hypostasizable in the way human nature is.
Quantity retains a natural inclination to a subject even when existing on its own.
An irrational nature can be assumed into unity of hypostasis but not of person.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e903.summary: Qualifies and continues the reply. An accidental nature such as quantity is neither rational nor hypostasizable by a divine supposit, so it cannot be assumed into unity of person or of hypostasis. He addresses the claim that an accident can inhere only in what it informs. Quantity could exist in God without informing him, more properly 'existing' than 'inhering', as quantity exists in the Eucharist without informing. An accident relates to a subject either as to something in potency to it, which implies imperfection, or as to its cause. In the second way God can sustain quantity without being informed or perfected by it, as he sustains all things as their cause (Augustine, on Genesis).
claims: Quantity cannot be assumed into unity of person or hypostasis.
An accident can relate to a subject either as to a potential recipient or as to its cause.
God can sustain quantity as its cause without being informed or perfected by it.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e975.summary: Reply to the anticipated rejoinder that dependence and informing are inseparable. Dependence extends further than informing and is prior to it. The assumed human nature depends on the Word's supposit without informing it, and the Eucharistic quantity depends on a sustaining principle without informing any subject. So quantity could depend on and be supported by the Word without informing it.
claims: Dependence is broader and prior to informing.
The assumed human nature depends on the Word without informing it.
Quantity could depend on the Word's supposit without informing it.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e1004.summary: Reply to the opposing opinion's first reason. A determinate form requires determinate matter, and the intellective soul's matter is an organic body. This holds of the soul as the natural philosopher considers it. Considered metaphysically, man can exist, and human nature can be assumed, without any quantity.
claims: The soul's need for an organic body holds of it as a natural being, not as a metaphysical one.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e1040.summary: Reply to the second reason. Man as a metaphysical being includes the whole quiddity of animal. To be sensible belongs to an animal in potency and by natural inclination, not in act, and such a man would keep the aptitude for sense organs. He could still actually understand, because the ordering of sensation before intellection belongs only to nature as now constituted. God could change that order (Hugh of St Victor) and present himself as object to such a man's intellect. The need for sensation reflects animal imperfection.
claims: Being sensible belongs to animal in potency and by inclination, not necessarily in act.
A man without quantity could understand without sensing.
The priority of sensation to intellection belongs to the present order of nature, which God can change.

olm8ij-g51791-d1e1101.summary: Reply to the third reason. If it held, quantity could not be separated from substance, since quantity determines its immediate subject, yet it is separated in the Eucharist. A proper attribute such as risibility cannot exist without its subject because it is only an aptitude, not a distinct absolute nature. Quantity is a distinct nature and can exist on its own. The soul determines an organic body for itself only in its physical, not its metaphysical, being.
claims: A proper attribute cannot exist without its subject because it is not a distinct absolute nature.
Quantity is a distinct absolute nature and can exist without substance.
The soul requires an organic body only as a physical being.

olm8ij-g51791-Dd1e121.summary: The single article asks whether a divine person could assume a man without quantity. Opponents say no. A determinate form like the intellective soul needs an organic, quantified body. Man is per se an animal, hence sensible, hence organic. The soul determines quantity in its matter. Aureol, seeing no contradiction, answers yes by distinguishing two ways of considering man. As a natural being, the object of natural philosophy, man includes quantity and quality in his definition (Aristotle, Averroes) and cannot be assumed without them. As a metaphysical being, composed only of matter and substantial form, he can be, because the soul's relation to the body as form is prior to its relation as mover and can give first being without second acts. Such a man would be neither wholly natural nor wholly metaphysical, since he would keep a natural inclination to quantity, like the separated soul. Aureol supports this ad hominem from his opponents' view that matter can exist without form: substance and quantity form a weaker, accidental unity, have distinct divine ideas, and stand as capable to capacity. Answering the opening arguments, he holds that dependence is broader than informing. God can sustain an accident as its cause without being perfected by it, as in the Eucharist and in the hypostatic union. Sensation's priority to intellection belongs only to the present order of nature.
claims: A divine person could assume a man without quantity, since no contradiction is involved.
As a natural being man includes quantity; as a metaphysical being he does not.
The soul's relation to the body as form is prior to its relation as mover.
A man assumed without quantity would be neither wholly natural nor wholly metaphysical.
Substance can exist without quantity more easily than matter without form.
Dependence is broader than informing; God can sustain an accident without being informed by it.
The priority of sensation to intellection belongs to the present order of nature, which God could change.

olm8ij-g51791.summary: Question 1 of Aureol's commentary on Book III, Distinction 23 (printed under the running title 'On the mode of union on the part of the one assuming') has a single article: could a divine person assume a man without quantity? Against opponents who tie the intellective soul necessarily to a quantified organic body, Aureol argues that it is possible. He distinguishes man as a natural being, whose definition includes quantity and quality, from man as a metaphysical being, composed of matter and substantial form. The second can be assumed without quantity, because the soul informs the body before and independently of moving it. Such a man would be intermediate between natural and metaphysical being. Aureol strengthens the case ad hominem from his opponents' admission that matter can exist without form. He also holds that an accident can depend on a sustaining cause without informing it, as in the Eucharist and in the Word's assumption of human nature.
claims: A divine person could assume a man without quantity.
Man considered metaphysically does not include quantity in his notion.
Dependence on a supposit does not require being informed by it.
